According to Mark Gurman's latest "Power On" newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making a series of changes to the App Store. The goal? To increase its potential revenue.

It remains unclear exactly what changes Apple plans to make to the App Store. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to increase profits and squeeze more recurring revenue out of the platform," an effort being primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

Allegedly, this is one of the reasons Phil Schiller, a long-time Apple veteran, departed the company last week. After stepping down as SVP of Marketing in 2020, Schiller became an Apple Fellow, with part of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. He did not agree with the concept:

Apple actually has plenty of ways it could increase App Store profits. It could do away with the costly human app review process, which isn't even that effective in the age of agentic coding. Further automating app review, though, might upset users, but it would certainly save money.

SF HOT TAKE

Considering Apple is one of the most valuable, yet erratic, companies in the world, this is absolutely terrible news if true and totally unnecessary. This could be a very bad sign from the incoming CEO. I was hoping a hardware guy running the company might bring Apple back to a time when they cared more about products than services, but this would just be plain avarice. I hope this isn't true.

Apple could raise the fee on its developer membership, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers are paying $200 per month for subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build their apps, you might think Apple could raise the price without losing subscribers. Apple could also charge larger developers subscription fees based on traffic to subsidize some of the infrastructure costs.

Only time will tell how this all plays out, but I'm definitely curious to see what these changes might look like.
